doc.title: Frank Foster and Bill Hughes interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Schenectady, New York, March 28, 1995

title: Throwaway themed albums of the 1960s
summary: Movie-theme and James Bond albums were done for money with outside arrangers who missed the Basie style.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: I was going to ask you how those kind of albums came about, like I know you did one of Hollywood movie themes too.
Oh, yeah, “The Apartment,” etcetera, etcetera. And the James Bond— I wasn’t in the band when these —

We were covering everything that wasn’t covered in the mid-60’s, I mean like doing record dates like often. A lot of the stuff that we went into the studios and did we’d sit there and we’d rehearse it, we’d record it, and that would be the last time we’d see that music.
I mean those kind of throwaway dates that Basie did, and it was all in the name of money, I think at that point.
Yeah, I think he was persuaded by the producers to do it, but on the gigs you never heard—
No, he wouldn’t play those tunes.
I thought, I personally thought that the James Bond album had the wrong arranger.
I don’t know. I really don’t know.

No, it wasn’t me though, right. See because a lot of these things were done and it seemed as though it was hard to fit the concept of the Basie style behind these charts. And they just didn’t come off. And the person who did the arranging was outside the band, of course, and didn’t really know Basie’s personal formula.
I don’t remember who recorded, I mean who wrote that album.
No, I don’t. I don’t recall who wrote. I remember doing the album.
